summaries.example: Imagine the sentence “The dog is eating all the treats.” By itself, we may not know which dog or which treats. An interpretation supplies those details. If one particular dog and group of treats make the sentence true, that interpretation is a model of the sentence. If the treats change tomorrow, the same sentence might no longer be true in that model.
summaries.summary: Model theory is the study of how languages are interpreted using structures made from objects and groups of objects. A sentence divides possible interpretations into those where it is true and those where it is not. The true interpretations are its models. A group of sentences can describe a whole class of structures, such as structures with addition and zero that follow familiar rules. Model theory also asks whether one sentence follows from others: this happens when every model of the earlier sentences is also a model of the conclusion. It compares the expressive strength of languages, meaning what each language can say. These ideas help with mathematics, logic, databases, computer programs, diagrams, and the study of meaning. The entry also distinguishes model theory from ordinary scientific modelling, where a model is often a theory about a real-world system.
key_ideas: Model theory studies how sentences get meanings and when they are true in particular structures.
A sentence can describe a class of all the structures that make it true.
A theory is a group of sentences that can define a kind of mathematical structure.
Different languages can express different amounts of information.
Model theory is related to logic, mathematics, computer science, and questions about meaning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Model theory gives us a careful way to ask what words and symbols mean, when statements are true, and whether a conclusion really follows from some rules. It helps mathematicians describe kinds of structures and helps computer scientists compare query languages and ways of representing information. It also raises philosophical questions about how we refer to mathematical objects and how formal languages connect with ordinary language and scientific theories.

important_terms.definition: A way of supplying meanings or references for the words and symbols in a sentence.
An interpretation that makes a sentence true.
A labeled collection of objects and groups of objects used to interpret a sentence.
A collection of sentences or rules used together to describe a class of structures.
What is true in every structure that makes all the sentences in a theory true.

questions_to_think_about: Can one sentence be true in one interpretation but false in another?
What details must be supplied before a sentence is clear?
Why might one language be able to describe more things than another?
How are a mathematical model and a model used to describe a real-world system different?

summaries.example: Consider the first-order language with symbols +, −, and 0. Give it the domain of all integers and their usual meanings. The sentence saying that addition is associative, that 0 acts as an identity, that every number has an additive inverse, and that addition is commutative is true in this structure. Other structures can also satisfy the same sentences; together they form the class of models of that theory. The formula v1 + v1 = v2, however, is evaluated after assigning particular objects to its variables: (−3,−6) satisfies it in the integers, while (3,3) does not.
summaries.summary: Model theory began as the study of formal languages, their interpretations, and the classifications those languages can make. In its mathematical form, a structure supplies a domain and interpretations for a signature’s predicate, function, and constant symbols. A sentence is true or false in a structure, and its models form a class that the sentence defines. A set of sentences, or theory, defines the structures satisfying them all. Model theory also studies definable relations within a fixed structure, interpretations of one structure in another, and different senses of definability. For a theory T and sentence φ, T entails φ when every model of T satisfies φ. In first-order logic, completeness links this semantic relation to formal proof, but questions about logical consequence remain philosophically significant because formalization may omit conceptual relations present in ordinary reasoning. The entry compares expressive strength across languages and describes back-and-forth games as a tool for showing that first-order logic cannot distinguish certain structures. Its expressive profile also enables nonstandard analysis: compactness can produce a model agreeing with the real-number structure on first-order claims while containing infinitesimals. Finally, the entry separates these technical models from theories used to model phenomena, while showing how model-theoretic ideas influence science, computing, cognition, and philosophy.
key_ideas: Model theory treats interpretation, truth in a structure, and definability as central mathematical notions.
A theory defines a class of models, while formulas can define relations inside one fixed structure, sometimes using parameters.
In first-order logic, the completeness theorem connects semantic consequence with formal provability, although broader logics require separate care.
Expressive strength compares what different languages can define; first-order logic is powerful about finite patterns but limited in distinguishing infinite sizes.
Compactness and expressive weakness support nonstandard analysis, where a structure can satisfy the same relevant first-order sentences as the real numbers while containing infinitesimals.
Model theory also informs databases, computer specification, natural-language semantics, diagrams, and philosophical questions about reference and mathematical practice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Model theory connects precise mathematical syntax with structures in which statements are evaluated. It provides tools for defining algebraic classes, testing semantic consequence, comparing languages, and understanding what formal systems cannot distinguish. Its applications include database queries and abstract state machines, while its philosophical importance comes from questions about reference, interpretation, isomorphism, indiscernibility, and the choices mathematicians make when formalizing a subject. The distinction between model-theoretic models and scientific modelling also prevents a common ambiguity in the word “model.”

important_terms.definition: A formal language contains logical symbols, variables, and nonlogical symbols whose meanings are supplied by a structure.
A set-theoretic arrangement of a domain together with labeled interpretations of a language’s nonlogical symbols.
A structure in which a sentence, formula, or theory is true under the relevant assignments.
A set of sentences that axiomatizes the class of structures satisfying all of them.
A sentence is a model-theoretic consequence of a theory when every model of the theory is also a model of that sentence.
The range of distinctions or classes of structures that a language can define.
A model of a fully interpreted statement that is mathematically allowed but not the intended interpretation.
A method for comparing structures by checking whether two players can distinguish them in a finite back-and-forth game.

questions_to_think_about: Does a formal consequence test capture every connection that speakers recognize as logical, or can conceptual analysis reveal more?
Why might a language that expresses more be less useful for some task than a weaker language?
What does a nonstandard model suggest about the difference between intended meaning and formal satisfaction?
How should we distinguish a model-theoretic structure from a scientific model that explains a phenomenon?
Can model theory clarify how mathematical objects are identified if we cannot interact with them causally?

summaries.example: Suppose a school database records students and clubs. One query-language sentence might ask, “Are there students who belong to every club?” A structure for the database supplies the students, clubs, and membership relation. The query is true in that structure if the relation makes the sentence true. If another language can express a more exact question, such as whether exactly three students belong to a club, that language has greater expressive strength for this task. A language limited to broad forms such as “All A are B” may not express the same detail.
summaries.summary: Model theory examines how language is interpreted through structures. A structure supplies a domain and assigns meanings to the symbols used in a sentence. The sentence is then true or false in that structure; a structure that makes it true is a model. A theory is a collection of sentences, and its models are the structures that satisfy all of them. This gives a precise way to define mathematical classes, such as structures obeying rules for addition, and to define relations inside a fixed structure, such as the points on a circle. Model theory also studies how one structure can be interpreted within another by using definable sets, relations, and sometimes equivalence classes. Model-theoretic consequence asks whether every model of some premises is also a model of a conclusion. In first-order logic, the completeness theorem says that this semantic idea matches formal proof, but formalization can miss connections that become visible only after we analyze the meanings of concepts. The entry compares languages by expressive strength: one language is stronger for a task if it can describe distinctions another cannot. Back-and-forth games help show when a language cannot tell two structures apart. These ideas have uses in databases, computer science, semantics, and nonstandard analysis. The entry also warns that a model-theoretic model is not identical to a scientific model, which is often a theory designed to describe or explain a phenomenon.
key_ideas: Model theory studies meaning and truth by examining sentences in structures, not just sentences by themselves.
The same sentence may be true at one time or place and false at another if the structure includes those features.
A theory can define a class of structures, while a formula can define a relation within one structure.
Logical consequence is modeled by truth in every permitted interpretation, but good formalization may require analyzing concepts first.
Languages differ in expressive strength, and this matters for database queries and other information systems.
Model theory has a technical meaning of “model” that differs from a theory used to model a physical event or planned system.
summaries.why_it_matters: Model theory shows how rules, meanings, and structures fit together. It helps explain why a mathematical definition can describe an entire class of objects, why a conclusion may follow in every allowed interpretation, and why some languages can express questions that others cannot. It also encourages careful thinking about the word “model,” which can mean a structure satisfying sentences, a theory about a real system, or a representation used in computing or reasoning.

important_terms.definition: The process of giving words or symbols specific meanings by connecting them with objects, groups, or relations.
A structure that makes a sentence or group of sentences true.
A labeled arrangement of a domain and relations, functions, or named objects that gives a language its meaning.
A group of sentences treated as rules or axioms for describing a class of structures.
A statement that is true in every model of the starting theory or premises.
How much a language can distinguish or describe compared with another language.
A structure that satisfies a formal statement but is not the interpretation originally intended.
A method of comparing two structures by seeing whether one player can force a difference to appear while the other tries to match moves.

questions_to_think_about: If a sentence is true in every model of a theory, is that enough to call it logically necessary?
Why might a sentence need information about time, place, or possible situations before it can be evaluated?
What kinds of questions can a powerful database language ask that a simpler one cannot?
Could two different structures agree on every statement in a limited language but still differ in important ways?
Why can a formal model and a scientific model both be useful even though they are not the same thing?
